versions.text:
On Saturday mornings the market hall at Ostrel smells of rind and wet stone, and for ninety years its business has turned on one object: a brass beam scale at the far end of the room, facing the glass case by the hall door where the market keeps its old iron weights. A farmer carries a wheel of cheese to the scale, the weigher calls the weight aloud, and buyer and seller strike their bargain on that number. The buyers are village families, shopkeepers from up the valley and, lately, restaurant buyers who drive up from the city of Tessaly before dawn.

For thirty-eight years the weigher was Anselm Dray. Ask the vendors why the public weighing matters and most will say the brass scale is truer than the stall scales they keep at home. Ask the council and you will hear that the weighing fee, a few coins a wheel, has paid for the upkeep of the hall since 1934. Mira Coll, a Tessaly sociologist who has studied the market for two years, calls the weighing the one habit that draws the whole valley into one room. Dray's answer was plainer. He would set a wheel on the pan, wait until the beam settled, and only then speak. “Everybody hears the same number at the same moment,” he told me. “Called aloud, a weight belongs to the buyer as much as to me.”

Dray announced his retirement two winters ago, and the council had to decide what came next. His niece, Tamsin Dray, had stood at his elbow on Saturdays since she was fourteen and had learned the scale from her uncle, down to the half-turn he gave the pan before every wheel. Odile Sarr, who chairs the council, came to its first meeting with a supplier's brochure for a digital scale to replace the brass one and a quote for what it would cost to buy one; she had already pictured the brass scale moved into the glass case by the hall door. Jory Ambel, a young goat-cheese maker, spoke for letting vendors weigh at their own stalls, and a letter from the restaurant buyers asked for a fixed price, so that the market would price each wheel as a whole.

That spring the council borrowed a digital scale for a month and set it beside the brass one. Its speed pleased almost everyone. The queue, which on busy mornings grew too long and reached the hall door, shrank to a handful of people, and the vendors who had complained of lost sales when buyers gave up and went home stopped complaining. That month an inspector from the provincial weights office tested both machines. He found the brass beam within a gram of true, which surprised only Jory, who had been saying for a year that it was out of true and reading light.

Coll had been reading the market's sales ledgers, which go back to 1934, and the trial month stands out in them. Wheels crossed the digital scale faster than they ever had, yet fewer were sold. Buyers took the quick number, then stood at the stalls haggling over it, as if a figure on a screen had told them little. “Speed was what everyone said they wanted,” Coll said. “The ledgers say they wanted to hear the weight called.” Sarr had figures of her own that summer, showing that the city restaurants had become the market's largest buyers, but it was Coll's pages the council kept returning to.

In June the council voted to keep the brass scale and to hand it to Tamsin. The brochure, Sarr told me, stayed in her bag. What decided the vote was the half-turn: a weigher who had learned the scale from her uncle was already standing beside it, trained, and the buyers knew her voice. The fee still pays for the upkeep of the roof, Tamsin still weighs any disputed wheel twice, and Jory still checks his cheese on his own stall scale before he brings it in, as most vendors do.

I went back on a Saturday in October. The queue reached the hall door, as it always has on busy mornings, and the people in it seemed content to wait. Tamsin lifted a wheel, gave the pan its half-turn, paused, and called the weight aloud, and a restaurant buyer who would weigh the same wheel again in one of Tessaly's kitchens nodded as though he had heard a verdict. Markets seldom lose a custom all at once; they lose the people who know how it is done. Ostrel kept its custom because one such person was already standing at the scale, and its council had the sense to see her.

The buyers were village families, shopkeepers from up the valley and, lately, restaurant buyers who drive up from the city of Tessaly before dawn.

For thirty-eight years the weigher was Anselm Dray. Ask the council why the public weighing mattered and you will hear that the weighing fee, a few coins a wheel, paid for the upkeep of the hall from 1934 on. Mira Coll, a Tessaly sociologist who has studied the market for two years, calls the weighing the one habit that drew the whole valley into one room, and buyers like to say they trusted a weight they heard called aloud. Dray's answer was about the brass itself. Accounts were settled at the hall door once the weighing was done, and he liked to say that in thirty-eight years no buyer had come back to complain. “The stall scales drift with the weather,” he told me. “This one is truer than any of them.”

Dray announced his retirement two winters ago, and the council had to decide what came next. His niece, Tamsin Dray, had stood at his elbow on Saturdays since she was fourteen and had learned the scale from her uncle, down to the half-turn he gave the pan before every wheel. Odile Sarr, who chairs the council, came to its first meeting carrying the letter in which the restaurant buyers asked for a fixed price, and a sheet of her own sums showing what each cheese would fetch if the market were to price each wheel as a whole. Jory Ambel, a young goat-cheese maker, spoke for letting vendors weigh at their own stalls, and a supplier's brochure for a digital scale to replace the brass one went round the table with a quote for what it would cost to buy one.

That spring the council borrowed a digital scale for a month and set it beside the brass one. Its speed pleased almost everyone. The queue, which on busy mornings grew too long and reached the hall door, shrank to a handful of people, and the vendors who had complained of lost sales when buyers gave up and went home stopped complaining. That month an inspector from the provincial weights office tested both machines. The brass beam, he found, was out of true; worn at its pivot, it had been reading light, putting every wheel a little under its real weight.

Coll had been reading the market's sales ledgers, which go back to 1934, and after the inspector's visit she reread them. The hall's weights could be set against the weights the dairies record when a wheel leaves the press, and for at least eleven years the hall's figures had run a steady fraction under the dairies'. “It was small enough to vanish in any single sale,” Coll said. “Over a decade it was the whole margin of a small farm.” Sarr had figures of her own that summer, showing that the city restaurants had become the market's largest buyers, but it was Coll's pages the council kept returning to.

In June the council voted to buy a digital scale of its own. Tamsin, who had offered to keep the brass scale, was asked instead to run the new one, and the habits her uncle had trained into her carried over. Sarr's sums went back into her folder. What decided the vote, she said, was the inspector's report: a beam worn out of true would have to be recast, and recasting it would cost more than a new scale. The fee still pays for the upkeep of the roof, Tamsin still weighs any disputed wheel twice, and most vendors still check their cheese on their own stall scales.

I went back on a Saturday in October. The queue was short even on a busy morning. Tamsin set each wheel on the digital pan and read the figure from the screen; she still calls it aloud, out of habit, though everyone can see it. The brass scale has been moved into the glass case by the hall door, its beam wired level. The restaurant buyers, who weigh every wheel again in their kitchens, tell me the numbers now match to the gram. Waiting my turn, I caught myself looking past the screen to the case, the way you glance at a chair someone used to sit in. The lesson Ostrel took is a sound one, that a market should have its scale tested before it trusts it. I only wish the test had come out the other way.

Coll had been reading the market's sales ledgers, which go back to 1934, and noticed something in the hours. Each sale is entered with its time, and on busy Saturdays the entries thin sharply after nine o'clock, just when the queue is longest, then recover once it clears. Most who vanish are families with small children. “They come, they see the line, they give up and go home,” Coll said. “You can read the lost sales in the gaps.” Sarr had figures of her own that summer, showing that the city restaurants had become the market's largest buyers, but it was Coll's pages the council kept returning to.

In June the council voted to let vendors weigh at their own stalls, with Tamsin, trained by her uncle, keeping the brass scale at the far end of the hall for any disputed wheel. Sarr's draft notice was folded away. What decided the vote, she told me, was the queue: a market that sends families home on its busiest mornings is shrinking, however fine its customs. The fee went with the public weighing; the council's general fund now pays for the roof's upkeep. The digital scale went back to its supplier, and the restaurant buyers still ask for a fixed price.

I went back on a Saturday in October. The vendors were weighing at their own stalls on scales of every age and make, and the long queue was gone. At noon a woman carried a wheel across the room to the brass scale, because the vendor's number and her own kitchen scale disagreed. Tamsin weighed it in silence and wrote the figure on a slip, and the vendor handed back the difference. Hers was the only line of the morning. Ostrel was right to time how long its buyers wait, and a market facing the same choice should do the same. But I kept counting stall scales that had gone a whole summer unchecked, and wondering how many wheels it takes before a buyer stops making that walk.

Dray's answer was about the room. When he lifted a wheel the whole hall settled, talk dropping away at every stall. “Without it they would order by phone,” he told me. “This brings the whole valley into one room once a week, and it is the only thing that does.”

The restaurant buyers were the exception: they still learned what a van-load cost only at the end of the morning, long after the drive up. Mira Coll, a Tessaly sociologist who has studied the market for two years, had been reading its sales ledgers, which go back to 1934. Fifteen years ago restaurants barely appear in them. By last year the six city restaurants that send buyers up the valley were taking more wheels than all the village families together, making them the market's largest buyers. “They are the market now,” Coll said. “Everyone else is shopping at it.” Sarr had figures of her own from the trial month, on speed and on how buyers felt about hearing a weight called, but it was Coll's pages the council kept returning to.

In June the council voted to stop weighing altogether and to price each wheel as a whole on a board beside the hall door. Sarr's draft rule went into a drawer. What decided the vote, she told me, was the restaurant buyers' letter: the market's largest customers wanted a fixed price before they set out, and a market that loses them closes. Tamsin, who had learned the brass scale from her uncle and was trained for a job that has since vanished, now chalks up the prices and sizes up any disputed wheel by eye.

I went back on a Saturday in October. The queue was gone, and so was the hush; the brass scale still stands at the far end of the room, a fern in its pan. The restaurant buyers came early, read the board and drove off. A week later, in a Tessaly restaurant, I watched a chef set each Ostrel wheel on a digital scale and log its weight, to work out what he had really paid by the gram. Every restaurant I visited does the same in its kitchens. Ostrel gave up weighing to please its largest buyers, and its largest buyers now do the weighing two hours down the valley, where nobody calls the number aloud. The advice still holds: ask your largest buyers how they would rather pay. Just expect them to start weighing once they have it.
